title: Roaming rubbish bin robot at Shinjuku Station solves the problem of where to put your trash
description: Japanese railway company comes up with a cute solution to one of the biggest problems for overseas tourists. As much as Japan is all about convenience and the spirit of hospitality, one thing that continues to confound visitors to Japan is the lack of trash cans. This can be particularly frustrating when you’re travelling and […]
content:
Japanese railway company comes up with a cute solution to one of the biggest problems for overseas tourists.

As much as Japan is all about convenience and the spirit of hospitality, one thing that continues to confound visitors to Japan is the lack of trash cans. This can be particularly frustrating when you’re travelling and enjoying the sights, because one piece of trash can quickly accumulate when you have no way to properly get rid of it.

It’s a problem that has long affected tourists as they eat and drink their way around all the different neighbourhoods, but now East Japan Railway (JR East) is coming to the rescue with a uniquely Japanese solution that not just solves the problem but is also fun to use.

The answer comes in the form of a rubbish bin that comes to you. Though that might sound crazy, it really is what the company is proposing, as it will be literally rolling out several mobile rubbish bin robots inside Shinjuku Station.

Each robot is designed to look like a train, with wide eyes on the front to attract the attention of passersby, and small nods to Shinjukuma, JR Shinjuku Station’s bear character, on the wrap.

The robot will automatically travel around the underground concourse on the first basement level – inside the East, West, Central East and Central West ticket gates – with openings on its sides for people to discard rubbish into as it passes by.

▼ The circular route.

The robot itself is an autonomous delivery robot capable of travelling both indoors and outdoors, developed by U.S. company Cartken and operated by Melco Mobility Solutions and Mitsubishi Electric.

JR East says the trial aims to improve service quality at stations while also making cleaning work more efficient, but the bigger question being addressed is whether a robot can actually navigate the crowds inside Shinjuku Station, which is often likened to a video game dungeon due to its expansive, labyrinthine layout.

The trial will examine how safely the robot can travel using its sensors and other onboard technology, as well as what problems arise when the station gets crowded. JR East will also look at whether the robot affects the movement of passengers through the concourse and how readily people accept the idea of having a mobile rubbish bin robot operating inside the station.

Shinjuku Station is known for being the busiest railway station in the world, so JR East is jumping into the deep end with the robot by trialling it under the most congested conditions. If the robot gets the green light after navigating this type of environment, we may see these little characters roaming around more stations in Japan in future.

For now, the trial is scheduled to take place on weekdays between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m., from 8 September to 20 November inside Shinjuku Station’s first-floor basement concourse. So if you have plans that will take you through the station during your travels, it might be worth holding onto your rubbish in the hopes of a robot encounter.

title: Ghibli’s Toshio Suzuki not impressed by generative AI images, Hayao Miyazaki thinks even less of them
description: As usual, Miyazaki doesn’t have time for anything that runs counter to his artistic principles. Almost as soon as generative AI image-making applications became something that the public had easy access to, “Ghibli-style AI illustrations” started getting shoveled into online spaces. Longtime fans of Ghibli that appreciate the studio’s human ethos in making art ground […]
content:
As usual, Miyazaki doesn’t have time for anything that runs counter to his artistic principles.

Almost as soon as generative AI image-making applications became something that the public had easy access to, “Ghibli-style AI illustrations” started getting shoveled into online spaces. Longtime fans of Ghibli that appreciate the studio’s human ethos in making art ground their teeth in frustration, while unconcerned technophiles were happy to have a way to avoid the thought and effort involved in the creative process and skip right to having a free facsimile of the basest elements of Ghibli aesthetics.

Studio Ghibli itself was pretty quiet on the whole subject, but company cofounder and longtime anime film producer Toshio Suzuki recently shared his thoughts on the use of AI to copy the Ghibli art style, and, in a sense, also shared how fellow Ghibli co-founder and director Hayao Miyazaki feels about it.

“When [Ghibli-style AI images] first started showing up online, I got asked about it a lot,” says Suzuki. “But I figured everyone would get tired of them pretty quickly. Sure enough, that’s what’s happened.”

Whether the loss of interest is quite as universal as Suzuki says could be debated, but postings of Ghibli-style AI images do seem to grab less attention these days. The ability of AI to generate images is no longer a novelty in and of itself, the obvious aping of the Ghibli house style rubs many of the more passionate fans of the studio the wrong way. But with AI capabilities continuing to advance, is Suzuki worried about it being used to create not just still images, but animation as well?

Not particularly. “AI can create certain types of animation, but people with a moderate amount of intelligence can see right through it. There’s not really much point to it. It’s not interesting or compelling.”

OK, so Suzuki clearly isn’t impressed or worried about generative AI. How, though, does Miyazaki, someone equally famous for his creative and curmudgeonly sensitivities, feel? Suzuki says “Miya-san doesn’t know what generative AI is in the first place.”

That might be a bit of a hyperbole on Suzuki’s part. At the very least, from a linguistic standpoint, “generative AI” is pretty straightforward, and despite his luddite leanings, Miyazaki must at least be aware that computers can now be used to generate images, so Suzuki’s comment might be a tongue-in-cheek way of saying that the director has such little interest in generative AI that he has no knowledge of it beyond the basic concept. Whether Suzuki is speaking literally or not, though, it’s clear that Miyazaki, as is so often the case, doesn’t really care what the rest of the industry is doing, and is as committed as ever to making his art his way.

It’s worth taking into consideration that Studio Ghibli, and Miyazaki in particular, enjoy a very unique position within the anime industry, and the entertainment industry as a whole, for that matter. Their unparalleled consistency in creating movies that are both critical and commercial successes mean that Ghibli can take all the time it wants to make its anime, and the involvement of Miyazaki is likely the only collateral needed to secure financial backing. Ghibli’s track record and prestige also mean that it can attract Japan’s top animator talent whenever it needs to gear up for a new project. Studios and directors whose resumes aren’t filled with modern classics, on the other hand, probably feel much more intense deadline and budget pressures, and thus stronger temptations from the presumed cost and time savings of AI, even if artistic quality suffers as a result.

Ghibli, though, has the option to quietly ignore generative AI, and Suzuki says that even if it becomes more prevalent in the industry, Ghibli will still be there as an example of the cultural value that can only come from human-made art.

title: Eel sauce is our new favorite cooking hack for making any dish sweet and savory with zero hassle
description: Here are five app-eel-ing side dishes, rice bowls, and sweets for using up your leftover eel sauce. Unagi no tare (うなぎのたれ), literally “eel sauce,” has become our favorite all-around sauce. While the product may or may not contain small amounts of eel extract itself, it’s intended to be a perfectly thick, glossy accompaniment for grilled […]
content:
Here are five app-eel-ing side dishes, rice bowls, and sweets for using up your leftover eel sauce.

Unagi no tare (うなぎのたれ), literally “eel sauce,” has become our favorite all-around sauce. While the product may or may not contain small amounts of eel extract itself, it’s intended to be a perfectly thick, glossy accompaniment for grilled eel made from a simmered blend of soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar. Many commercially prepared versions exist, such as the one from Japanese brand Nihon Shokken, pictured below.

▼ Nihon Shokken’s eel sauce

This particular one does contain a tiny amount of eel extract but it’s not one of the top three ingredients. From the top those are soy sauce, mizuame (a Japanese sweetener), high-fructose corn syrup, and mirin, all ahead of the extract.

It was one of these bottles that we had purchased for use in one recipe but ended up having a decent amount of leftover sauce. Not wanting to waste it, we began experimenting with what we could use it on besides eel. It turns out that the sky is the limit when it comes to eel sauce’s potential–here are five ways to add it to easy Japanese homestyle dishes and snacks.

1. Grilled onigiri (rice balls)

First up is an easy and satisfying snack. Simply mix the eel sauce into the rice before shapjng the onigiri. We also threw in some leftover green onions and roasted sesame seeds for extra flavor.

Grill the onigiri in a pan or air fryer until you start to see faint scorch marks on the rice. The resulting snack has a deeper and richer taste than if using soy sauce alone.

2. Oyakodon (chicken and egg rice bowl)

Oyakodon is a hearty and delicious homestyle meal packed with protein and flavor. Begin by boiling the eel sauce with some water before adding chunks of chicken and onions. Let simmer until mostly cooked, then add in the beaten egg. Lay the mixture over a bed of rice to complete the dish.

The resulting eel sauce version was amazing, and involved less hassle than measuring out the individual ingredients for the simmering stock alone. We may always just use eel sauce from here on out.

3. Japanese amberjack

We actually picked this recipe up from food company Yamada Suisan’s YouTube channel. Grill the fish in a pan for a bit before adding equal amounts of eel sauce and water. Let simmer until the liquid is reduced.

It was an extremely simple dish involving hardly any prep. The cooked appearance was shiny and enticing, and while we enjoyed it very much, we also wished there was just a tiny bit more added sweetness. We’ll just make a mental note for next time.

4. Hard-boiled eggs

If you’re looking for a way to liven up your eggs, this is an easy hack for doing so. Let hard-boiled eggs with the shells removed soak in a closed bag with some eel sauce for about half a day. The resulting salty-sweet edge it provides is a perfect accompaniment for the eggs.

5. Mitarashi dango (glazed rice dumplings, usually skewered)

Add a small amount of water to some eel sauce in a pan and turn on the heat. We also added a tiny bit of potato starch to thicken it. When the sauce becomes viscous, add in some boiled-then-chilled shiratama dango (rice flour dumplings).

A quick taste test of the resulting mitarashi dango led us to add some kuromitsu (brown sugar syrup) to enhance the sweetness. That seemed to do the trick, so we recommend adding nearly equal amounts of eel sauce and either kuromitsu or sugar to make for a sweetly tantalizing dessert.

There you have it–five simple dishes to make using your leftover eel sauce. In fact, you probably wouldn’t even know they contained eel sauce if no one told you, since the overall ingredients are commonly represented in a variety of Japanese simmered and teriyaki dishes. Nihon Shokken’s eel sauce did leave us personally wanting to add a bit more sugar to the dishes at times, but this may not be the case with other brands or based on personal preferences.

We love finding novel ways to turn leftover ingredients into yummy new creations. Here are some of our top picks, from the weird to the wonderful.

title: New Shinkansen platform vending machine sells local-flavor treats from 127-year-old snack maker
description: A new way to get your hands on a popular souvenir at Shin Osaka. There’s a good chance you’re in a hurry if you’re about to hop on the Shinkansen. After all, the bullet train network is generally the fastest option for long-distance travel in Japan, often even quicker than flying since it doesn’t require […]
content:
A new way to get your hands on a popular souvenir at Shin Osaka.

There’s a good chance you’re in a hurry if you’re about to hop on the Shinkansen. After all, the bullet train network is generally the fastest option for long-distance travel in Japan, often even quicker than flying since it doesn’t require a time-consuming side trip to an out-of-the-way airport or lengthy check-in process.

And if you’ve got a full schedule of places to go and things to see, speedy snack procurement is also important, so now there’s a special Shinkansen platform vending machine in Osaka offering a popular local-flavor snack.

This bright yellow box at Shin Osaka Station is stocked with Osaka Ikaten, and for the uninitiated bears the in-English explanation that they’re “sea squid cradcker[s].” That might seem redundant, considering the lack of land squid in our world, but the “sea” part is probably included because these snacks are made by Bunkaku Sohonpo, a maker of seafood senbei (rice crackers) that’s been in business since 1899.

▼ Osaka Ikaten

Bunkaku Sohonpo is best known for their flagship Yukari brand of shrimp crackers, and shrimp are among the ingredients for Osaka Ikaten. The main draw here, though, is squid (ika in Japanese), which is accompanied by shiso (Japanese basil). Fans say the combination makes Osaka Ikaten deliciously flavorful, but without any harsh acridity that would give your taste buds mixed feelings about the eating experience.

Bunkaku Sohonpo is actually based in Nagoya, but when fans of their snacks in Osaka began asking for a special version, the company looked to Osaka’s food culture for inspiration. As a city of unabashed hearty eaters, Osaka has a number of foods it’s associated with, but ikayaki was the one that Bunkaku Sohonpo felt it could best honor with its particular kind of expertise. While in most parts of the country ikayaki simply refers to grilled squid, often served sliced and skewered, Osaka ikayaki is a little different, looking more like a folded squid dumpling or pancake.

Since its debut 11 years ago, Bunkaku Sohonpo’s Osaka Ikaten has become a popular souvenir among travelers in Osaka, and the Shin Osaka Station vending machine, which went into service last month, makes it even easier to pick up a pack either as soon as you arrive in the city or right before you leave. The machine is located on the platform shared by Lines 25 and 26, near where Car 9 of the Shinkansen trains stop, and offers a 12-pack of Osaka Ikaten for 950 yen (US$6) (cashless payment only). And if you’re looking for more unique vending machines in the same station, there’s another one just one platform over.

title: Japanese restaurant chain offering free food for a year if you beat massive meat bowl challenge
description: A stamina bowl of legendary size could save you a ton of money on future meals. Before we get to the meat of this story, let’s start with a little linguistic appetizer. Japanese restaurant chain Densetsu no Sutadonya’s name translates to “Legendary Sutadon Shop.” So what’s sutadon? An abbreviation of “stamina donburi,” or “stamina rice […]
content:
A stamina bowl of legendary size could save you a ton of money on future meals.

Before we get to the meat of this story, let’s start with a little linguistic appetizer. Japanese restaurant chain Densetsu no Sutadonya’s name translates to “Legendary Sutadon Shop.” So what’s sutadon? An abbreviation of “stamina donburi,” or “stamina rice bowl.”

Sutadon, also known as stamina-don, are rice bowls with an extra-large portion of meat seasoned with a copious amount of garlic, as both foods are considered to be energy boosters among Japanese foodies. And if all that has your mouth watering and stomach demanding a sutadon as soon as possible, you’ll be happy to know that Densetasu no Sutadonya has recently started offering its newest creation: the Legendary-Size All-Star Sutadon. You might then be unhappy to learn that it costs 4,990 yen (US$31), several times more than a normal stamina bowl, but your spirits will probably perk up at the fact that eating this could be a massive financial gain for you, since it could win you free food for an entire year.

Let’s take a look at what comes in the Legendary-Size All-Star Sutadon.

In addition to the rice, you get:
● A quintuple-size portion of Densetsu no Sutadonya’s simmered garlic pork
● Three mincemeat cutlets
● Two chicken cutlets
● Four pieces of nanban karaage (fried chicken with tartar sauce)
● A cheese omelet
● Curry sauce with cheese
● 10 slices of takuan (pickled daikon radish)
● Shredded cabbage
● Sliced green onion

The contents of the Legendary-Size All-Star Sutadon weigh in at a collective 3.5 kilograms (7.7 pounds), so this is not a meal for the faint of heart or small of stomach. If you can manage to finish the whole thing within 35 minutes, though, Densetsu no Sutadonya will reward you with not only an acrylic mini standee of the Legendary-Size All-Star Sutadon, but also with “one year of free sutadon.”

There isn’t much fine print available on the announcement, but ostensibly this would mean, at the very least, one free standard stamina bowl per day for a full calendar year. With Densetsu no Sutadonya charging 930 yen for that menu item, a year of freebies would work out to a value of 339,450 yen. That would make for a profit of 334,460 yen, or roughly a 6,700-percent return on your initial investment of 4,990 yen, far beyond the performance any stock portfolio could ever hope to achieve in a year’s time.

▼ Heck, that’s a better return on investment than even the unattainable ones that crypto scams promise.

▼ The standard-size stamina bowl is no measly sized snack, either.

Obviously, Densetsu no Sutadonya can’t just whip up a Legendary-Size All-Star Sutadon on a moment’s notice, nor are all of their kitchens prepared to put together something of this size. Because of that, it’s only available by advance reservation of one week or more at participating branches, which are the Shinjuku Nishiguchi, Akihabara, Koenji, Akishima, and Ikebukuro branches in Tokyo, as well as the Nagareyama Otaka no Mori (Chiba), Sapporo Eki-mae (Hokkaido), Sendai Nakakecho (Miyagi), Dotonbori (Osaka), and Fukuoka Tenjin (Fukuoka) branches. Those willing to bet on themselves/their bellies can make reservations online here, with eating dates available through September 23.

title: How to watch Studio Ghibli’s new anime in Japan, with a special after-dark outdoor screening for Halloween
description: First-ever nighttime screening takes place in the real-world setting for A Night in the Valley of the Witches. This autumn looks set to be a very good time to be a Studio Ghibli fan in Japan, as there are a number of special events scheduled to be held at the studio’s theme park in Aichi […]
content:
First-ever nighttime screening takes place in the real-world setting for A Night in the Valley of the Witches.

This autumn looks set to be a very good time to be a Studio Ghibli fan in Japan, as there are a number of special events scheduled to be held at the studio’s theme park in Aichi Prefecture.

The first thing to make fans smile is the screening of a brand new Studio Ghibli short directed by Hayao Miyazaki’s son Goro, who also serves as park director. Called Majo no Tani no Yoru, or A Night in the Valley of the Witches, the film has been co-directed by Akihiko Yamashita, the character designer and animation director for several Ghibli films, including Howl’s Moving Castle.

▼ Howl’s Moving Castle, as seen inside Ghibli Park.

With this being the first new Ghibli short anime since 2018, the film has already been attracting global interest, but there’s only one place in the world where you can see it – at Ghibli Park. The short began screening in the park’s Orion cinema in July, and although the 170-seat theatre usually rotates through a series of 10 other Ghibli shorts on a monthly basis, the park has confirmed that the short will continue screening through September and October.

This is great news for Ghibli fans who missed out on seeing the film in summer, and the park has another extra special treat in store for its youngest fans, as it will be holding its first-ever outdoor nighttime screening of A Night in the Valley of the Witches, exclusively for elementary school-age children.

▼ This one-night only event will be held in Valley of Witches, which serves as the real-world setting for the film.

According to the official synopsis, the movie follows a “new guy” who has just been hired to work at Ghibli Park. After a series of requests to repair its buildings, he encounters some unexplained phenomena, which leaves him spooked, but his senior colleague Kikue doesn’t seem fazed by it at all. Then, one night after the park closes, the new guy heads to Valley of Witches to work the night shift for the first time, and there he sees Kikue in a cloak, who tells him: “I’m a witch.”

▼ She begins chanting a spell, and when she swings her lantern down… the magic begins.

Though this magical story usually plays out on the screen of the Orion cinema within the Grand Warehouse complex, the special nighttime screening is set to take place in the great outdoors, giving little ones the space for their imaginations to run free against the backdrop of the witch-themed park area.

▼ Valley of Witches is home to a number of buildings with connections to Ghibli’s witchy films, including this recreation of the Okino Residence from Kiki’s Delvery Service.

Though parents are required to accompany their children into the park, the outdoor screening is said to be strictly for elementary school-age children only. Once parents drop their kids off at the Valley of Witches, the children will watch the 14 minute, 21 second short and then be led around by staff on a special after-hours tour, which the park says will include dark areas, loud noises, and light effects. The event runs from 6 to 7:30 p.m. on 31 October, and although it’s free, advance applications , with a 110-yen (US$0.72) booking fee, are required here from 20 to 28 September.

Of course, if you’re not a child, you’ll still be able to watch the new animated short inside the Orion cinema throughout September and October, as long as you have an entry ticket to the park that includes the Grand Warehouse (you can purchase tickets from overseas here or locally here). To add to the fun, there’ll also be some special events taking place as part of the annual “Autumn Dondoko Festival” which runs from 30 October to 22 November this year.

Some of the events planned for the festival include a late closure on 30 October, when Valley of Witches and Mononoke Village will stay open until 7 p.m., allowing visitors to experience both areas after dark. Valley of Witches will also start its winter illuminations on the same day, giving the area a completely different feel compared to a daytime visit.

▼ Mononoke Village

On 1 November, Ghibli Park will celebrate its anniversary with an outdoor screening of Porco Rosso at 5:30 p.m. and a concert on the park grounds featuring Tokiko Kato, the singer who performed the theme song for Porco Rosso and also voiced Gina in the film. Both the concert and screening are free, although advance applications are required here (tickets to the park are not a requirement) and a lottery will be held if numbers exceed capacity.

▼ Tokiko Kato

There will also be a series of workshops and events on weekends in November, including lessons in how to paint backgrounds in the style of a Ghibli anime on 7-8 November, a workshop where visitors can make their own cafe tray using the same tiles found on the Grand Warehouse’s central staircase on 14-15 November, and a new workshop where participants can create their own one-of-a-kind Totoro plush toy, to be held on 21-22 November. These events also require advance reservations, although no separate park tickets are required, with details set to be made available here at the end of September.

So if you’re in Japan this autumn, you’ll want to put Ghibli Park on your list of places to visit. And don’t forget to hitch a ride on the Catbus while you’re there!

title: We tried Japan’s Wobbly Beer Glass that forces you to drink water, and it humbled us
description: This classy drinking session didn’t go quite as planned. Just last month, we wrote about an unusual beer glass developed by Yo-Ho Brewing, the Japanese company behind popular craft beer brand Yona Yona Ale. Called the “Furatsuku Beer Glass” (“Wobbly Beer Glass”), the unusual U-shaped vessel is designed to hold beer in one side and […]
content:
This classy drinking session didn’t go quite as planned.

Just last month, we wrote about an unusual beer glass developed by Yo-Ho Brewing, the Japanese company behind popular craft beer brand Yona Yona Ale. Called the “Furatsuku Beer Glass” (“Wobbly Beer Glass”), the unusual U-shaped vessel is designed to hold beer in one side and water in the other, encouraging you to drink both in equal measures to make the wobbly glass stand upright and prevent it from toppling over.

▼ This ad for the product shows how it works.

While it looked impressive in the commercial, we had doubts about how well it might work in an everyday drinking session, and although we wanted to try it for ourselves, the 13,750 yen (US$85.99) price tag was a pretty big barrier to entry.

So when our reporter P.K. Sanjun opened a parcel in the office the other day, from an old colleague who now works at Yo-Ho Brewing, we all gasped in surprise as he pulled out the U-shaped glass, giving us the chance to see it in action firsthand.

▼ It comes with a convenient stand for safe and secure storage.

Placing it gingerly on the desk, P.K. was surprised to see that it did manage to balance on its own, even when empty – as long as the two sides have equal amounts of liquid, and in this case none, it will stay upright.

Excited to see whether he could master the unusual glass and enjoy his beer in a more sophisticated fashion, he gave it a quick wash and then prepared his water and beer.

▼ Keeping the glass steady in the stand, he filled one side with beer, and then the other with water.

▼ Now all he had to do was sit back and enjoy the beer, but…

▼ … it wasn’t easy to drink from.

Not only was the act of drinking hard physically, it was also hard mentally. Usually, when P.K. opens a beer it’s to unwind and relax, but there was no relaxing with this glass in his hand. He was so worried about the possibility of liquid from the other side splashing onto his forehead while he drank that he found himself stretching his neck into uncomfortably strange positions.

▼ Keeping a constant eye on the liquid levels was a bit of a stressful distraction, but thankfully no liquid splashed in his face.

Without realising it, P.K. ended up holding the glass for an unusually long stretch of time, as if something in the back of his mind was telling him not to sit it down on the table. However, the Wobbly Glass’s balancing act is all part of its unique charm, so he couldn’t finish his beer without at least giving it a try.

Carefully sipping on both sides until he had what seemed to be an even balance, he carefully set it on the table and…

▼ … success!

It balanced beautifully on the desk, tipping slightly towards the fuller end of the glass, as if pointing out that he’d drunk less water than beer. Feeling slightly bad about his lax water consumption, he dutifully picked up the glass and finished both the water and the beer.

He then took the glass over to the sink to wash it out, and lamented the fact that it didn’t come with a specially designed brush to make the job of cleaning a little easier.

As he washed the glass, he was able to gather his thoughts on the drinking experience, and came to the conclusion that perhaps the problem wasn’t the glass, but him. For more cultured souls, who like to elegantly sip on craft beers, a glass like this can be a pleasing source of entertainment, and even an exciting challenge to test their abilities, kind of like the way Guinness drinkers like to try and “Split the G“, by gulping the beer in one go until the surface sits in the middle of the G on “Guinness” on the pint glass.

For P.K., though, splitting the U in two, by drinking it from either side so it balances, wasn’t a fun and easy task – in fact, he describes it as a hectic experience – but that’s probably because he felt so worried about breaking the glass and not using it properly that he let it all get to his head. He’s the kind of guy who doesn’t mind a nice tipple, but he now knows that if you add a fancy glass into the equation, he breaks out in a bit of a sweat.

So in the end, P.K. might not have what it takes to be a sophisticated drinker, but he did say that the glass made him drink more water than he ever would have otherwise, and that is the point of the glass, after all. title: Legendary Pokémon statues installed in downtown Tokyo, will be there through the fall
description: Legend Research event brings more than 100 Pokémon species to the Tokyo Station area. content:
Legend Research event brings more than 100 Pokémon species to the Tokyo Station area.

Within the Pokémon games and anime, Pokémon Trainers who are looking for the most powerful species of Pocket Monsters need to venture to remote locations far outside human settlements. However, right now in the real world there are over 100 Pokémon, including more than a dozen Legendary Pokémon, waiting to be found in downtown Tokyo.

The Pokémon Legend Research event kicked off this week in the Nihonbashi and Yaesu neighborhoods, located just east of Tokyo Station. For the next two and a half months, visitors to the Coredo Muromachi, Tokyo Midtown Yaesu, and Nihonbashi Mitsui Tower shopping and restaurant complexes will be able to spot artwork displays of more than 100 different types of Pokémon.

謎解きをはじめとするさまざまな体験が楽しめるよ。
くわしくはこちらをチェックしてね！https://t.co/yzpujYlP5v pic.twitter.com/e43SBTttnV

— ポケモン公式 (@Pokemon_cojp) September 9, 2026

While some of those are two-dimensional illustrations, there will also be 19 Pokémon statues, representing the original-generation starter trio’s final evolved forms, Venusaur, Charizard, and Blastoise, plus several Legendary Pokémon such as Lunala, Solgaleo, and Groudon, Xerneas, Zacian, Zamazenta, and, Ho-oh.

In addition to looking awesome, the statues are also part of a mystery game that fans can play, as each one features a hidden code that can be used in conjunction with your phone to solve a multi-stage puzzle. There’s no mention on the event’s website of a prize, but it seems like there must be some sort of reward for those who manage to complete it, since participating in the game requires a 3,300-yen (US$21) ticket which can be purchased online.

There’s no charge at all to see the statues, though, as they’re all situated in publicly accessible parts of the three entertainment complexes. Skipping the mystery-solving game will also allow you to instead spend that money on some of the new merch on offer at the Pokémon Legend Research popup shop inside Tokyo Midtown Yaesu, such as folding fans, tote bags, mugs, and key chains.

Pokémon Legend Research in Nihonbashi and Yaesu will be going on between now and November 29, and should you need a refresher on what the featured Pokémons’ names are, there’s a song that’ll teach you what each and every species is called.

title: Tokyo’s Rikugien Garden announces nighttime foliage illumination event ahead of autumn
description: Stroll among the illuminated autumn leaves after-hours in one of Tokyo’s most popular Japanese landscape gardens for only one and a half weeks. content:
Stroll among the illuminated autumn leaves after-hours in one of Tokyo’s most popular Japanese landscape gardens for only one and a half weeks.

From November 25 through December 6, one of Tokyo’s nine Metropolitan Gardens will be open for a special autumn foliage illumination event. Doors will close at the typical time of 5 p.m. but will reopen between 6 and 8:30 p.m. for visitors to soak in the magical nighttime atmosphere.

Rikugien is an Edo-period (1603-1868) Japanese landscape garden located in northern Tokyo with easy access from the JR Yamanote Line. It’s particularly famous during the spring and fall months for its cherry blossoms and foliage respectively, but it’s truly a gem year-round.

▼ Rikugien in its summer glory

©SoraNews24

Several small teahouses dot the grounds, where you can enjoy matcha and wagashi (traditional Japanese sweets) while taking in the views.

▼ The scenery from Fukiage Chaya

©SoraNews24

▼ Matcha and wagashi

©SoraNews24

If you’re lucky, you may even have the privilege of encountering a local who’s also taking a stroll around the well-manicured paths.

©SoraNews24

To celebrate the garden’s seasonal transformation in late November, illuminations and other decorations will be added throughout the grounds, especially centered on the autumn leaves and small islands dotting the pond.

Of particular note will be a handful of special photo spots that are perfect for commemorating your visit.

New to this year will be a projection mapping attraction in the bamboo grove near the former storehouse.

Once you’ve worked up an appetite from all the walking around, you can even take a moment to relax at the Fukiage Chaya and Shinsentei teahouses, or indulge in some light food and drinks at one of the stalls and food trucks that will be available near the site of Ginkatei for the duration of the event.

Entry for the special nighttime illumination event is 1,000 yen (US$6.39) for advance tickets (online only) or 1,200 yen for day-of tickets (online or in-person; cash only). Admission for children in elementary school and younger is free. You may want to also track Japan’s recently released “fall color forecast” to maximize your leaf-peeping opportunities in the coming months.

title: Japan’s 20-year Ig Nobel winning streak continues thanks to people blowing their noses
description: Learn the scientifically proven technique for blowing your nose efficiently. Science has tackled many a mystery for the advancement of human knowledge and understanding, from black holes to gene editing, but there are some researchers out there who turn their focus to the more mundane and humorous things in life and ask themselves, “What is […]
content:
Learn the scientifically proven technique for blowing your nose efficiently.

Science has tackled many a mystery for the advancement of human knowledge and understanding, from black holes to gene editing, but there are some researchers out there who turn their focus to the more mundane and humorous things in life and ask themselves, “What is going on here?” To laud the value of the efforts of those people, the Ig Nobel Prizes came into being, celebrating achievements that first make you laugh, and then make you think.

This year, in the 36th installment, and the first time being held in Switzerland, the Ig Nobel Prize in Medicine went to the late Dr. Tokuji Unno, Professor Emeritus at Asahikawa Medical University, and Dr. Hiroshi Yajima for their 1977 study: How to Blow the Nose. This marks the 20th consecutive year that a Japanese researcher has won one of the Ig Nobel Prizes.

▼ Here Dr. Miki Takahara of Asahikawa Medical University accepts the award on behalf of Dr. Unno who passed away in 2022, but you can also enjoy the entire award ceremony itself.

While nose blowing seems like an everyday occurrence, Unno and Yajima wondered whether people were actually blowing their noses properly. So, with pneumotachometers (airflow meters) and eardrum pressure transducers, they hooked up 15 volunteers to dissect the aerodynamics of the common honk.

Their mechanical breakdown of the human nose blow revealed crucial data for nasal hygiene enthusiasts everywhere:

● The One-Side Policy
Nasal passages are rarely created equal, and blowing both barrels at once causes airflow to take the path of least resistance. To clear the clogged side, you must block the clear side to build up a high-velocity airstream.

● The Power Blow
A commonly held thought was that blowing hard is bad for the ears, but the airflow inside the nose and middle ear infections are separate issues. Higher flow velocity increases the discharge efficiency of built-up mucus.

● The Long Blow
The average blow lasts 1.23 seconds and ejects 1.34 liters of air, which is about a third of your vital lung capacity. To maximize clearance right down into the bronchia, take a moderate breath in and execute a sustained, steady blow rather than a short, hyper-pressurized burst.

▼ Modest blows are not going to clear those sinuses efficiently.

The Ig Nobels are a humorous reminder that even the most mundane of daily habits are governed by fascinating physics. The next time you reach for a tissue, you can press one nostril, and blow long and proud with scientific confidence.

title: Megadeth guitarist becomes voice of reason regarding tourists dancing at shrine in Japan
description: Tourists’ dance video at Kyoto shrine prompts angry response from Marty Friedman. There are times in life when agreeing to disagree is the most sensible thing to do, but so too are there times when someone has to be willing to stand up and say “What you’re doing is wrong, so stop.” Sometimes that voice […]
content:
Tourists’ dance video at Kyoto shrine prompts angry response from Marty Friedman.

There are times in life when agreeing to disagree is the most sensible thing to do, but so too are there times when someone has to be willing to stand up and say “What you’re doing is wrong, so stop.” Sometimes that voice comes from political or spiritual leaders…and sometimes it comes from the former lead guitarist of thrash metal band Megadeth.

At this point, it’s probably safe to say that just about anyone who’s looked into traveling to Japan has seen photos of Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari Shrine. Founded in the year 711, Fushimi Inari is the head shrine of all those dedicated to Inari, the Shinto god of rice, commerce, and foxes, among other dominions. The shrine is also famous for its thousands of torii gates along the walking paths that connect its lower buildings with other structures higher up the mountain behind them, and this picturesque element has made Fushimi Inari one of the most popular destinations in all of Japan for foreign tourists.

With modern tourism being what it is, though, a place can no longer be a top travel destination without also being seen as a prime social media backdrop, and any place that’s seen as a prime social media backdrop is, unfortunately, also going to attract people who’re so excited about trying to look cool that they might not take the time to consider whether or not they’re being respectful. That brings us to a Twitter post by former Megadeth guitarist Marty Friedman regarding a dance video recorded by some foreign tourists at Fushimi Inari.

Dear tourists: PLEASE STOP DOING THIS. Japan is known for gracefully welcoming foreigners, but those days will end if you continue this disrespect. You are leaving an extremely shameful impression of your entire country. Who raised you to act this way? Just stop. Thank you. https://t.co/zV7OBXlI50

— Marty Friedman (@marty_friedman) September 6, 2026

Now, those who haven’t checked in on what Friedman’s been up to since leaving Megadeth might look at his stern message of “PLEASE STOP DOING THIS. Japan is known for gracefully welcoming foreigners, but those days will end if you continue this disrespect,” and assume that his opinions on Japanese culture carry no more weight than a random Tokyo sushi chef’s pontifications on guitar technique. However, Friedman has actually been living in Japan for more than 20 years, and it’s not like he’s spent all that time in an expat-enclave bubble, as he speaks the local language well enough to be a contributor to Japanese TV talk shows and music magazines. The guy’s been here long enough to know what he’s talking about when he says that Japanese society isn’t cool with tourists using shrine grounds in this way, and that behavior like this carries the risk of souring locals’ perceptions of international visitors in general.

Friedman’s post is a reply to another tweet criticizing the video, saying that the shrine is “sacred ground” and “not a backdrop for social media content,” which itself warrants some discussion about something that can be hard for foreign tourists in Japan to grasp.

Many of Japan’s religious sites do not have or cultivate a heavily solemn atmosphere. The streets leading to major shrines and temples are often lined with restaurants and souvenir shops, and a mood of levity isn’t seen, in and of itself, as sinful or inappropriate, even on shrine/temple grounds. The sprawling layout of sites such as Fushimi Inari can also contribute to a casual atmosphere, as moving about the spaces between structures can feel like a walk in the woods or stroll in a garden. As such, while shrines and temples are religious sites, they might not necessarily feel like “sacred ground,” in that they don’t impose the same sets of strict regulations and restrictions that term might imply in other cultures. However, just because visitors aren’t expected to be somber at Japan’s shrines and temples doesn’t mean it’s OK for them to be flippant.

The original post’s admonishment that Fushimi Inari is “not a backdrop for social media” might be going a bit far, if one were take that to mean that shrines in Japan frown on any photos being taken on their grounds and then posted on social media. Many shrines and temples in Japan are famous for their seasonal flowers or foliage, and when the colors are at their prettiest, even many Japanese people will come for a visit and take photos. Generally speaking, things like snapping a quick photo with a friend in front of a cherry blossom tree or traditional architectural feature are fine. However, there’s a big difference between that and the sort of thing shown in the tweeted video, where a half-dozen or more people have tramped off the allowed footpath into the surrounding natural environment, then hop back in and block the entire walkway while they make that part of the shrine their group’s personal dancefloor, most likely with a tripod set up to record themselves and claim even more space as theirs.

Getting back to Friedman’s warning, it is true that for most of the modern travel era, Japan has been pretty understanding of foreigners’ faux pas. Even Japanese people are aware that there are a lot of subtle nuances to their culture’s etiquette systems, and that some of the finer points might not be readily apparent to people from other parts of the world. It becomes harder to forgive such impoliteness, though, when it’s done with self-satisfied exuberance.

But again, maybe some tourists just don’t have any warning bells go off in their heads before they film videos like the one shown in the tweet. It’s possible that they think “Well, I don’t see anyone praying right here, so it’s probably not a serious religious place, so I can do whatever I want, right?” Really, though, the rule of thumb when visiting cultural sites is that if there’s something that you don’t see any of the locals doing, such as filming a dance video on shrine grounds, then you shouldn’t do it either.

title: Family Mart releases 47 convenience store socks and stickers, one for every prefecture in Japan
description: New designs give us an insight into Japan’s prefectural flowers and regional gems. Travel in Japan is always an exciting journey of discovery, especially when there are 47 prefectures, each with their own regional specialties to explore. Now there’s even more to discover, as Japanese convenience store chain Family Mart has just revealed a massive […]
content:
New designs give us an insight into Japan’s prefectural flowers and regional gems.

Travel in Japan is always an exciting journey of discovery, especially when there are 47 prefectures, each with their own regional specialties to explore.

Now there’s even more to discover, as Japanese convenience store chain Family Mart has just revealed a massive new range of 47 socks and stickers, with designs that capture the charms of each prefecture. Each design can only be found at Family Mart stores within the prefecture it represents, making the products very sought after, and worth travelling for.

▼ The 47 socks, arranged according to the prefecture in which they can be found, creating the shape of Japan.

There’s a lot to get through here, so let’s start by taking a look at the socks, which are based on Family Mart’s iconic Line Socks, known for their stripe designs. In the new collection, the colour of the stripes varies by prefecture, as a nod to its prefectural flower.

The first 14 prefectures, and their flowers, are: Hokkaido (Japanese Rose), Aomori (Apple Blossom), Iwate (Paulownia), Miyagi (Thunberg’s Bush Clover), Akita (Butterbur Sprout), Yamagata (Safflower), Fukushima (Nemoto Rhododendron), Ibaraki (Rose), Tochigi (Yashio Azalea), Gunma (Japanese Azalea), Saitama (Japanese Primrose), Chiba (Rapeseed Flower), Tokyo (Yoshino Cherry), Kanagawa (Goldband Lily).

One of the highlights in this lot of socks has to be the Tokyo version, which uses brown, green, and various shades of pink to capture the look of Somei Yoshino, Japan’s most widespread variety of cherry blossom.

▼ The back of each pack comes with a sweet illustration and some details about what the design represents.

The next nine in the series are: Niigata (Tulip), Toyama (Tulip), Ishikawa (Fritillaria), Fukui (Narcissus), Yamanashi (Pigmy Cherry), Nagano (Japanese Gentian), Gifu (Chinese Milk Vetch), Shizuoka (Azalea), Aichi (Rabbit-ear Iris).

Next up, we have 12 that include big cities like Osaka and Kyoto: Mie (Japanese Iris), Shiga (Rhododendron), Kyoto (Weeping Cherry), Osaka (Japanese Primrose), Hyogo (Wild Chrysanthemum), Nara (Double Cherry Blossom), Wakayama (Japanese Apricot), Tottori (Nijisseiki Pear Blossom), Shimane (Tree Peony), Okayama (Peach Blossom), Hiroshima (Japanese Maple), Yamaguchi (Summer Orange Blossom).

Though Tokyo and Kyoto both pay tribute to the beauty of Japanese cherry blossoms, the types of sakura are slightly different, giving us two unique looks.

▼ Osaka’s prefectural flower brings beautiful purple hues to this design.

Finally, we travel further south, to prefectures on the islands of Shikoku, Kagoshima, and Okinawa.

Tokushima (Sudachi Citrus Blossom), Kagawa (Olive Blossom), Ehime (Orange Blossom), Kochi (Red Bayberry Blossom), Fukuoka (Japanese Apricot), Saga (Camphor Flower), Nagasaki (Unzen Azalea), Kumamoto (Japanese Gentian), Oita (Bungo Plum Blossom), Miyazaki (Grand Crinum Lily), Kagoshima (Kyushu Azalea), Okinawa (Coral Tree).

Moving on to the exclusive stickers, we travel the breadth of the country again, from Hokkaido to Okinawa, but this time we’re being introduced to some of the gems in each prefecture.

Hokkaido (Melons), Aomori (Apples), Iwate (Wanko Soba), Miyagi (Zunda Mochi), Akita (Namahage), Yamagata (Cherries), Fukushima (Kokeshi), Ibaraki (Natto ), Tochigi (Gyoza), Gunma (Daruma), Saitama (Soka Rice Crackers), Chiba (Peanuts), Tokyo (Business District), Kanagawa (Steamed Dumplings).

A closer look at the stickers reveals that the star portion adds a little something extra to each design. For the Tokyo sticker, an image of an arty manhole cover acts as a hat-tip to the many creative designs that exist around the city.

Namahage are demons that feature in Oga no Namahage, an annual event in Akita that’s been designated as a UNESCO intangible cultural heritage. The star beside the demon in this regional sticker symbolises the blade carried by the demons during the event.

Natto, Japan’s famously divisive fermented food, is featured in the sticker for Ibaraki, with a side of mustard in the star as a nod to the mustard that commonly comes with it.

Moving down the mainland, there’s plenty more to discover as we make our way into central Japan.

Niigata (Rice), Toyama (Medicine), Ishikawa (Wajima Lacquerware ), Fukui (Sauce Katsudon), Yamanashi (Peaches), Nagano (Oyaki), Gifu (Gohei Mochi), Shizuoka (Deep-Steamed Green Tea), Aichi (Fried Prawn).

Niigata is famous for rice, and the star here is said to resemble a pickled plum. Together, these two ingredients make up Hinomaru Bento, a boxed meal that replicates the Japanese flag (“hinomaru”), and is said to be best made with Niigata rice, given its excellent quality.

The sticker for Toyama might seem a little puzzling at first, but the prefecture has a long history of pharmaceutical production that can be traced back to 1690. You can even try some of the ancient machines used for pill-making in the prefecture today.

Next, we venture into Western Japan, which includes Osaka and Kyoto.

Mie (Spiny Lobster), Shiga (Shiga-ware Raccoon Dog), Kyoto (Maiko), Osaka (Takoyaki), Hyogo (Kobe Beef), Nara (Persimmon Leaf Sushi), Wakayama (Nanko Plum), Tottori (Nijisseiki Pear), Shimane (Magatama [comma-shaped beads]), Okayama (Momotaro [Peach Boy]), Hiroshima (Okonomiyaki), Yamaguchi (Fugu [blowfish]).

When you’re in Kyoto, you’ll want to keep an eye out for this homage to the apprentice geisha who call the city home. The star is designed to resemble a sanjufuda (votive slip), which can be seen on some of the shrines and temples around Kyoto.

Osaka is synonymous with takoyaki octopus balls, and the star here symbolises the red ginger that’s commonly eaten with them.

Finally, we make our way to Shikoku, Kyushu and Okinawa.

Tokushima (Awa Odori), Kagawa (Sanuki Udon), Ehime (Mikan), Kochi (Seared Bonito), Fukuoka (Tonkotsu Ramen), Saga (Hot Air Balloons), Nagasaki (Stained Glass), Kumamoto (Mustard Lotus Root), Oita (Onsen), Miyazaki (Mangoes), Kagoshima (Black Pork), Okinawa (Shisa).

Shisa are guardian lion-dogs, and they’re an important part of Okinawan culture that can be seen in many guises throughout the island chain.

So next time you’re travelling around Japan and stopping by Family Mart for a rice ball and an umbrella, be sure to keep an eye out for the exclusive socks and stickers. They’ll make for an ideal convenience store souvenir, and a great memento of your travels.

title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s remake can be played with an actual ocarina [Video]
description: Nintendo shows off its Switch 2 remake of the 1998 classic and plays songs three different ways. This year marks the 40th anniversary of Nintendo’s Legend of Zelda series, but for the biggest part of the celebration the company is actually looking back to 28 years ago. That’s when the franchise made the jump to […]
content:
Nintendo shows off its Switch 2 remake of the 1998 classic and plays songs three different ways.

This year marks the 40th anniversary of Nintendo’s Legend of Zelda series, but for the biggest part of the celebration the company is actually looking back to 28 years ago. That’s when the franchise made the jump to 3-D polygonal graphics for the first time with 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which is getting a remake for the Switch 2.

Nintendo teased the project with a single preview still back in June, but released further details late Tuesday night Japan-time as part of a Zelda Nintendo Direct. The video presentation included Eiji Aonuma, producer for the Ocarina of Time, playing through a portion of the game while providing commentary and highlighting what parts of the original it carries over and what additions players can look forward to.

The remake updates the controls and camera to fit with more modern preferences. Protagonist Link can now jump wherever and whenever he wants to with the push of a button, and the original game’s fixed camera angles have been replaced with the ability to freely position the virtual lens using the right analog stick. In terms of art design, Ocarina of Time looks to be following a similar course to Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Starfox 64 which came out earlier this year, aiming for a much more photorealistic look to its environments, and far more detail and less abstraction in its character designs, especially when compared to the cel-shaded style of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, the two most recent mainline Zelda games.

It’s probably going to be a divisive aesthetic choice, quite possibly the most so since 2002’s The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker. However, Aonuma also showed off something that’s likely to put a smile on any and all Zelda fans.

It’s not really a spoiler that Ocarina of Time features a magical ocarina that Link can play to activate certain powers. Within the original version of the game, you play different songs by hitting different buttons, and that holds true for the remake too.

But after playing a song the conventional way, Aonuma revealed that, since the Switch 2 controller has a built-in microphone, you can skip the button presses and instead hum the song you want to play, and Link will “hear” you and copy the notes on his in-game instrument.

▼ Note the “inputting audio” message.

Or, if you want to get really immersive, you can whip out an actual ocarina of your own and play that!

Assuming that the controller’s mic can pick up the sound of wind instruments as effectively as it can human humming, it would seem that, theoretically, you could play any ocarina. However, the one that Aonuma is seen using in the video is an official Ocarina of Time ocarina from video game peripheral maker Hori that’ll be going on sale through the Nintendo Store online shop.

▼ Aonuma demonstrating the three ways to play the Ocarina of Time in Ocaring of Time

No release date has been mentioned for the ocarina, but the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake comes out November 5.

Can these new character candidates match up to the charm of the penguin?

Last November, East Japan Railway Company (JR East) surprised everyone by announcing that it would be retiring its “Suica Penguin” mascot character on 31 March, 2027. The character has been the mascot for JR East’s tap-and-go Suica prepaid IC card system since it was first introduced in 2001, even appearing on the cards themselves, so the decision to “graduate” the character, to use the company’s terms, had everyone wondering if there might be a replacement mascot on the way.

▼ The last lot of IC cards with the Suica Penguin have already been shipped, signalling the end of an era.

Well, that question was answered today, when the company announced that it would indeed be replacing the penguin with a new character. What’s more, it’s come up with three candidates for the public to choose from, with votes being welcomed from people around the world, regardless of age, gender, location, occupation or nationality.

The three candidates were selected by a panel of judges from proposals submitted by young creators, with JR East looking for a character that could embody its vision for the future of Suica. The company hopes that the new character will represent the next stage of Suica’s “renaissance”, as it aims to expand its service from a tool primarily used for transportation and small payments into a broader “device for everyday life” that connects people and communities. The candidates were chosen for their potential to act as a “cute companion” that customers can feel connected to, and a friendly guide who can explain things in an easy-to-understand way.

▼ The three candidates have very different personalities… and a different look to the cute sophistication of the Suica Penguin.

▼ Option A is a squirrel.

According to the production notes, this character has a pattern on its body that forms one continuous line from the head all the way to the tip of its tail, like a railway line. Taking inspiration from the way JR East “connects Japan and the lives of people”, the character and its distinctive stripe are expressed with soft, curved lines to help it feel like a “friend who supports people and gently stays by their side”.

Selection committee comments:
“This character embodies the concept of ‘staying close to people’, combining friendliness and lovability.”
“Its rich expressions give the impression that a story could emerge from the character.”
“It could become a presence that is widely loved by customers and group employees.”

▼ Option B is a rabbit.

The production notes here highlight the symbolism of the rabbit in conveying a character that goes beyond the concept of transportation and connecting people and towns – by listening closely to the voices around it, the rabbit leaps forward into the future. This character aims to gently support people from different generations in an ever-changing world, helping to nudge them forward with a little encouragement.

The character’s purple hue is said to be created by mixing blue, which symbolises “suisui” (smoothness and reassurance), with red, which symbolises “wakuwaku” (excitement). Although the production notes don’t specifically mention it, it’s interesting to note that “suisui” actually served to inspire the word Suica, as it was chosen to evoke the idea of an IC card that lets you move about smoothly and easily.

Selection committee comments:
“This is a highly impactful and striking character.”
“An original character, and when animated, its ears would probably move, making it even cuter.”
“Because it has a freshness unlike anything seen before, it has the potential to be loved for many years to come.”

▼ Option C is… a mystery with a mole?

The final character is a bit of a mystery, with the production notes describing it as an orange character carrying a mole – an animal that lives underground that you don’t often get to see – in a pouch. The character, which to us kind of looks like it has the body of a penguin and the head of a koala, is said to want to show the mole various places, capturing the excitement of going out while expressing its gentle nature.

Selection committee comments:
“It has fluffy cuteness, yet also a dependable strength. It has a mysterious charm that makes you want to root for it.”
“I could relate to the simplicity of ‘I want to show you a world you’ve never seen before.’”
“It embodies Suica’s future concept of being a ‘companion that customers can feel close to.’”

▼ JR east has released this video, in Japanese, which includes comments on the characters from the selection committee.

Going by first impressions, these characters seem to have nothing on the beloved Suica Penguin, appearing much more crude and childlike by comparison. Although their backstories help to give them more depth, comments online have been largely critical of the candidates.

“The designs for the new characters all feel too low-budget to me.”
“I feel like if JR East’s corporate colour is green then none of them really match.”
“Ugh, this is even worse than I imagined. At this rate, it’d be better to go with no characters at all.”
“Are they seriously hiring professional illustrators for this? Or did they just cheap out and get some in-house person who’s only mildly decent at drawing to whip them up?”
“From a production point-of-view, I feel like A is probably the main contender and the other two are just decoys.”
“Even if you hire all three of then at once, you still can’t beat a single penguin.”

If you do want to see one of these mascots become the future face of Suica, and likely the character to be used on the new IC cards, then head on over to the official site and cast your vote. Votes are limited to one per person and can be cast from 3 p.m. on 8 September until 11:59 p.m. on 23 September. The winning character will be announced in November, after which time name suggestions will be taken, with the selection committee set to judge the name in January next year. In March, the character name will be announced, before the winning character takes over from the Suica Penguin on 1 April.

title: Converse Japan releases green tea cup sneakers so you can wear your love for sushi on your feet
description: All Star Yunomi Hi lets you step into the world of sushi. The world of Japanese sushi is as vast as the ocean, covering specialised tools, tableware, and a whole lot of fishy vocabulary. Now, there’s a way to take a bold step into that world, quite literally, with a new pair of kicks from […]
content:
All Star Yunomi Hi lets you step into the world of sushi.

The world of Japanese sushi is as vast as the ocean, covering specialised tools, tableware, and a whole lot of fishy vocabulary. Now, there’s a way to take a bold step into that world, quite literally, with a new pair of kicks from Converse.

Called the All Star Yunomi Hi, these unisex sneakers take the recently revamped All Star design and cover the canvas with neat rows of kanji. To the uninitiated, the kanji characters give the shoes a cool, Japanese-style look, but to sushi lovers, the layout of the characters, and what they signify, will be instantly recognisable.

▼ These kanji characters are a list of fish names, laid out in the same style as the yunomi green tea cups you see at sushi restaurants.

In amongst the many characters, you’ll find words like 鰯 (sardine) and 鯖 (mackerel), just as you might find on the traditional yunomi that inspired the shoes.

▼ Spot your favourite sushi names within the pattern.

There are a few surprises hidden amongst the fish kanji, though, because a closer look reveals stars, and the characters 全星 , which combines the kanji for “all” (“全”) with the kanji for “star” (“星”), as a nod to the Converse “All Star”.

▼ Step into these and you’ll feel like you’re the green tea, being poured into the teacup sneakers.

If these shoes look familiar, you might be thinking of a similar model that Converse released last year. However, that model used the older and more familiar All Star design, which had a white sole and toe box, with white canvas uppers and patch, whereas this one takes a step in a new direction, with navy details to make the kanji pop against the darker background.

It’s a fun take on the Japanese teacup, and a cool way to show your love for sushi as you stride around town. Just as green tea helps to make sushi taste great, these kicks will add a special little something to your outfit, and they can be purchased at the Converse online store and retail stockists around Japan from 25 September, priced at 11,000 yen (US$70.54).

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new Chilled Cup drinks for autumn
description: Roasted green tea is one of two exclusive flavours coming our way for a limited time. Starbucks has always been keen to reach as many customers as possible, and one way they’ve been doing that is through their “Chilled Cup” range. Sold at stores around the country since 2005, the range has given us a […]
content:
Roasted green tea is one of two exclusive flavours coming our way for a limited time.

Starbucks has always been keen to reach as many customers as possible, and one way they’ve been doing that is through their “Chilled Cup” range.

Sold at stores around the country since 2005, the range has given us a lot of flavour combinations, and now there are two new varieties joining the lineup for a limited time this autumn.

▼ The White Chocolat Latte and Hojicha & Tea Latte

The White Chocolat Latte, which takes its inspiration from Starbucks’ popular White Mocha, combines a hit of coffee with the richness of white chocolate for a very creamy, dessert-like drink. The depth of flavour in the coffee is said to balance out the sweetness for a harmonious, well-rounded flavour.

The design is just as enticing as the flavour, with imagery on the cup evoking the rich, meltingly sweet flavour inside, and splashes of purple giving the cup a luxurious feel.

The Starbucks Hojicha & Tea Latte is made with 100-percent domestically produced hojicha (roasted green tea). Sweet and creamy, the toasty notes from the hojicha give the drink a rich, fragrant flavour, with black tea added for a bright, aromatic accent.

The packaging here incorporates an autumn-leaf-inspired colour scheme and Japanese motifs to reflect the traditional hojicha flavour inside, while metallic embellishments add a shiny finish to catch the eye.

To make a moment of the drinks, Starbucks recommends enjoying the White Chocolate Latte with a chocolate chip cookie, as the contrast between dark and white chocolate enhances the richness of both.

For the Hojicha & Tea Latte, Starbucks recommends pairing it with a tuna and cucumber sandwich, saying the crisp cucumber and creamy tuna work to complement the roasted flavour of the tea.

Richer drinks like these are perfectly timed for cosy autumn days, and they’ll be available at a recommended retail price of 230 yen (US$1.45) at stores nationwide from 8 September.

title: Starbucks Japan proves Pumpkin Spice is NOT dead, with a new take for autumn
description: Exclusive lineup breathes new life into the Pumpkin Spice Latte, and serves up other designer beverages too.  There’s been a lot of talk recently about the death of Pumpkin Spice, with experts saying online data indicates the hype for it is over, as many young people turn to other drinks like matcha. Here in Japan, […]
content:
Exclusive lineup breathes new life into the Pumpkin Spice Latte, and serves up other designer beverages too. 

There’s been a lot of talk recently about the death of Pumpkin Spice, with experts saying online data indicates the hype for it is over, as many young people turn to other drinks like matcha.

Here in Japan, though, Pumpkin Spice is still alive and kicking, at least at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo, where it’s just been unveiled as part of the new autumn lineup.

Created around the theme of “Crafting a Playful Fall“, the five beverages in the range are born from the spirit of “craft exploration” that’s said to be deeply rooted in the Roastery Tokyo. While many will be interested in the new take on Pumpkin Spice, there’ll also be a lot of interest in the Espresso Rosso Tonic, as it was devised by Starbucks’ 19th Coffee Ambassador, Asumi Yamaguchi.

▼ Asumi Yamaguchi, the 19th Coffee Ambassador

▼ Espresso Rosso Tonic (1,178 yen [US$7.55] takeout, 1,200 yen dine-in)

Available at the Main Bar on the first floor, this drink is inspired by the espresso tonic, which Yamaguchi says was her gateway into black coffee, which she now loves. Created when she was competing in the Ambassador Cup, this new beverage combines coffee with brown sugar syrup, cinnamon, and passionfruit tea with a hint of cranberry for layers of unique flavour.

▼ Barrel-aged Pumpkin Spice Latte (1,400 yen, dine-in only)

While we await news of whether Pumpkin Spice will be gracing the menu at Starbucks branches around Japan this autumn, Reserve Roastery Tokyo is showcasing it in a beautiful latte, made with domestically grown pumpkin powder, and the Roastery’s “Whiskey Barrel-Aged Coffee” blend. Topped with iyokan peel, (iyokan is a tangerine-like Japanese citrus fruit), and a dash of cinnamon and nutmeg, this is a very unique drink that breathes new life into pumpkin spice.

Rounding out the autumn lineup are three other intriguing creations, with two tea-based specials up at the Teavana Bar on the second floor.

▼ Kaga Bo Hojicha Gelato & Tea (1,374 yen takeout, 1,400 yen dine-in)

Developed in collaboration with Teavana Bar baristas, this carefully designed beverage features Kaga Bo Hojicha gelato, made in-store. Paired with a fragrant and refreshing Kaga Bo Hojicha tea, a roasted green tea from Ishikawa Prefecture, this drink evolves as the gelato slowly melts, allowing you to enjoy the different dimensions of the roasted tea.

▼ Earl Grey Autumn Tea (Hot/Iced) – 1,080 yen takeout, 1,100 yen dine-in

This tea beverage combines the refreshing, autumnal taste of grapes with Earl Grey tea and spices like cardamom and ginger. The juiciness of the fruit and the elegant aroma of the tea are said to harmonise perfectly, creating a deep and complex flavour with every sip.

The collection is complete with a unique cocktail up at the third floor Arriviamo Bar.

▼ Honey Pear Brew (2,500 yen, dine-in only)

This coffee cocktail, also available in a non-alcoholic version, combines pear, mead (honey wine), and cold brew coffee. The fruity flavour of the pear, the richness of the honey, and the aroma of the cold brew create a delicious blend, ideal for long autumn evenings.

So if you’re looking to keep Pumpkin Spice alive this autumn, the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo is the place to go. If you prefer to treat your taste buds to different autumnal flavours, the other seasonal drinks in the multi-storey building will take them to new heights, and they’ll all be on the menu for a limited time from 4 September.

title: Anime magical girls grow to gigantic size with new Madoka Magica plushies [Photos]
description: Are you ready to commit to sharing your home with Madoka and Homura? Though its claim to fame is the dark twists it puts on the genre, Puella Magi Madoka Magica is still a magical girl anime, focusing on a cast of adolescents whose lives are changed when they receive their special powers. Incidentally, in […]
content:
Are you ready to commit to sharing your home with Madoka and Homura?

Though its claim to fame is the dark twists it puts on the genre, Puella Magi Madoka Magica is still a magical girl anime, focusing on a cast of adolescents whose lives are changed when they receive their special powers. Incidentally, in Japanese magical girls are called maho shojo, with shojo, meaning “girl” and written with the kanji characters 少女, which translate literally to “small woman.”

However, while Madoka Magica’s Madoka Kaname and Homura Akemi are both magical girls, and thus maho shojo, their new plushies are not at all small.

Sure, they’ve got the super-deformed proportions often seen in compact stuffed animals. But that sofa Madoka and Homura are sitting on in the above photo? That’s not doll furniture. As a matter of fact, that’s not even a kids-size couch, because these plushies are gigantic.

Posed in a seated position, these stuffed animals measure one full meter (a little over three feet and three inches) in height. That means that if they could stand, they’d be even taller, likely close to the height of an actual petite middle schooler like Madoka and Homura are within the anime.

▼ Homura here is big enough that it looks like she’s ordering the human to water her plants.

Madoka and Homura are the latest entries in manufacturor Taito’s Doqute series of jumbo-sized plushies, created to celebrate the release of Puella Magi Madoka Magica: Walpurgisnacht: Rising, the latest anime movie in the franchise which opened in Japanese theaters late last month. As the series has progressed, the franchise has become increasingly focused on the pair’s interpersonal relationship, so while the series started off with a core cast of five magical girls, the other three aren’t getting the Doqute treatment this time.

▼ Though that could possibly be because the designers know that there’d be no way to fit Doqute versions of all five of them in a room together.

While the SD-style aesthetics simplify the character designs down quite a bit, they still retain the series’ distinct sketch lines under the characters’ eyes.

As you can probably guess, these aren’t cheap, with each plushie having a price tag of 66,000 yen (US$415). Stores aren’t going to be stocking these on the off-chance that a random shopper will comes moseying in and grab one off the shelf, either. Instead, they’re being offered by pre-order only, between now and October 13, through the Taito Goods online shop here, with shipping slated for March of next year.

title: Tokyo’s red-light district cafe lets you dine inside a real 1960s cabaret
description: Used as a Netflix crime drama set, this safe, solo-female-friendly venue offers up black omurice and colorful retro sodas. Kabukicho, in Tokyo, is Japan’s most recognizable red-light district, packed to the brim with adult entertainment and touts for venues that charge exorbitant and unexpected fees. It’s not the sort of place where most travelers, women […]
content:
Used as a Netflix crime drama set, this safe, solo-female-friendly venue offers up black omurice and colorful retro sodas.

Kabukicho, in Tokyo, is Japan’s most recognizable red-light district, packed to the brim with adult entertainment and touts for venues that charge exorbitant and unexpected fees. It’s not the sort of place where most travelers, women in particular, would probably feel comfortable heading into an establishment alone and for the first time. However, we came across a Kabukicho cafe that even many solo women are keen to dine at, and it’s like stepping through a portal into a world set half a century prior.

Our Japanese-language reporter Natsuki Gojo is a lover of all things cute, with her life goal being to live surrounded by cute things, spread the charm of cuteness and become a cute grandmother. One of her less grandiose dreams, though, was to visit a Showa-era (1926–1989) cabaret, so when she found out about Niinana Kissa, a cafe that operates inside what used to be the famous Hinomaru Cabaret, she knew she had to be brave and venture forth into Kabukicho.

Walking through the district, just north of Shinjuku’s iconic Godzilla Head installation, Natsuki soon came across the cute retro sign…

…but the building itself was another mental hurdle for her to overcome, being less than warm and welcoming.

Pushing aside her trepidation, Natsuki plucked up her courage to walk up the stairs and open the door.

Unfolding before her was a glamorous Showa cabaret, with neon lights shaped like the Japanese flag (colloquially called the Hinomaru) dazzlingly brightly at the end of the room.

Looking up at the ceiling, it was covered in mirrors, and the disco ball was sparkling like a massive gemstone.

The entrance had, to put it bluntly, an intimidating vibe, but take a step inside, and it’s truly another world. Natsuki’s excitement couldn’t help but shoot through the roof, this was exactly the type of cabaret she had been longing to visit at least once.

Since Niinana Kissa was used as a filming location for the Netflix crime drama series Tokyo Swindlers, Natsuki was a little worried about what to do if there were scary customers inside, so just in case, she prepared some high-pressure fashionable sunglasses to adopt a don’t-mess-with-me vibe.

▼ They turned out to be completely unnecessary.

Looking around the interior, it was clear that the main customer base was groups of women, who all seemed to be enjoying oshikatsu (activities centered on supporting their favorite idol or character) by savoring colorful drinks, but there were also couples and women by themselves too. In fact, the typical Kabukicho-like clientele that Natsuki had been expecting wasn’t there, being mostly women and younger generations. Taking off her unneeded sunglasses, she settled in her seat and got ready to enjoy herself.

During peak hours, there is a 60-minute limit (or an additional order required), and after 10:00 p.m., a cover charge of 500 yen (US$3) applies, but during other time slots, you can use the cafe without a cover charge.

Having come all this way, Natsuki opted for the most popular drink and food to see the best the cafe had to offer.

▼ Although there were numerous tantalizing options to choose from.

The 27 Club Soda (900 yen) is just so photogenic, with a rich variety of versions available. Natsuki selected orange, which is said to be one of the most popular among customers because of its great taste.

On top of the refreshing orange soda, there’s whipped cream, ice cream, an Oreo, and a cherry, and while the menu says it’s a drink, it feels more like a dessert. Natsuki loved how voluminous it was, but she had to wrap up her photos quickly as the ice cream soon started melting.

Sipping on her drink, Natsuki admired the cuteness of both the coasters and the matchboxes.

The overwhelming favorite food is said to be the Black Omurice (1,500 yen), but with the amount of cheese sauce, it’s definitely more white than black.

▼ Oh… wait…. there it is.

The inside is pitch black. Unlike some other instances of black food being a result of including squid ink, this blackness comes from bamboo charcoal, and the lightly-seasoned rice goes exceptionally well with the rich cheese sauce. Due to how black it was Natsuki wasn’t quite sure what to expect as they took a bite, but the vegetables and meat still turned out to have a thoroughly enjoyable texture and flavor.

While there is a trend for photogenic items at places where you go to enjoy the space to not be particularly delicious, the menu at Niinana Kissa is genuinely tasty. In fact, whenever Natsuki feels like having something to drink or eating a meal around Kabukicho, she’s considering using it as a regular coffee shop.

▼ Even the sofas on the side look comfortable enough to enjoy some refreshments on.

For some, there is one thing that might put people off, and that is that smoking is allowed, though Natsuki could see that as adding to the sense of having traveled back in time to the Showa era.

Contrary to its somewhat intimidating exterior, Niinana Kissa is a charming space where, once inside, you can enjoy it in various ways, from reflecting on a bygone era to using it as an everyday cafe.
